source_text: „Ὁ θεὸς“ οὖν „δίδωσιν“ „ἑκάστῳ“ „σῶμα, καθὼς ἐθέ λησεν,“ ὥσπερ ἐπὶ τῶν σπειρομένων οὕτω καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν οἱονεὶ σπειρομένων ἐν τῷ ἀποθνῄσκειν καὶ καιρῷ ἐπιτηδείῳ ἀναλαμβανόντων ἐκ τῶν σπειρομένων τὸ περιτιθέμενον ἑκάστῳ κατὰ τὴν ἀξίαν „σῶμα“ ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ. ἀκούομεν δὲ καὶ τοῦ διὰ πλειόνων διδάσκοντος λόγου τὴν διαφορὰν τοῦ οἱονεὶ σπειρομένου πρὸς τὸ ὡσπερεὶ ἐγειρόμενον ἀπ᾿ αὐτοῦ καὶ λέγοντος· „σπείρεται ἐν φθορᾷ, ἐγείρεται ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ· σπείρεται ἐν ἀτιμίᾳ, ἐγείρεται ἐν δόξῃ· σπείρεται ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ, ἐγείρεται ἐν δυνάμει· σπείρεται σῶμα ψυχικὸν, ἐγείρεται σῶμα πνευματικόν.“ ὁ δὲ δυνάμενος ἔτι καταλαμβανέτω, τί νενόηται τῷ λέγοντι· „οἷος ὁ χοϊκὸς, τοιοῦτοι καὶ οἱ χοϊκοί· καὶ οἷος ὁ ἐπουράνιος, τοιοῦτοι καὶ οἱ ἐπουράνιοι. καὶ καθὼς ἐφορέσαμεν τὴν εἰκόνα τοῦ χοϊκοῦ, οὕτω φορέσωμεν καὶ τὴν εἰκόνα τοῦ ἐπουρανίου.“ καίτοι δὲ βουλόμενος κρύπτειν ὁ ἀπόστολος τὰ κατὰ τὸν τόπον ἀπόῤῥητα καὶ μὴ ἁρμόζοντα τοῖς ἁπλουστέροις καὶ τῇ πανδήμῳ ἀκοῇ τῶν διὰ τοῦ πιστεύειν ἀγομένων ἐπὶ τὸ βέλτιον, ὅμως ἠναγκάσθη ὕστερον ὑπὲρ τοῦ μὴ παρακοῦσαι ἡμᾶς τῶν λόγων αὐτοῦ εἰπεῖν μετὰ τὸ „φορέσωμεν τὴν εἰκόνα τοῦ ἐπουρανίου“ τὸ „τοῦτο δέ φημι, ἀδελφοὶ, ὅτι σὰρξ καὶ αἷμα βασιλείαν θεοῦ κληρονομῆσαι οὐ δύναται, οὐδ᾿ ἡ φθορὰ τὴν ἀφθαρσίαν κληρονομεῖ.“ εἶτ᾿ ἐπιστάμενος ἀπόῤῥητόν τι καὶ μυστικὸν κατὰ τὸν τόπον, ὡς ἔπρεπε διὰ γραμμάτων καταλιπόντι τοῖς μετ᾿ αὐτὸν τὰ νενοημένα εἰρημένα ἐπιφέρει καὶ λέγει· „ἰδοὺ μυστήριον ὑμῖν λέγω,“ ὅ τι περ ἔθος ἐστὶν ἐπιφέρεσθαι τοῖς βαθυτέροις καὶ μυστικωτέροις καὶ καθηκόντως ἀπὸ τῶν πολλῶν κρυπτομένοις· ὥσπερ καὶ ἐν τῷ Τωβὴτ γέγραπται· „μυστήριον βασιλέως καλόν ἐστι κρύπτειν,“ πρὸς δὲ τὸ ἔνδοξον καὶ ἁρμόζον τοῖς πολλοῖς μετὰ τοῦ οἰκονομικῶς ἀληθοῦς „τὰ ἔργα τοῦ θεοῦ ἀνακαλύπτειν ἐνδόξως“ „καλόν.“ οὐ σκωλήκων οὖν ἡ ἐλπὶς ἡμῶν οὐδὲ ποθεῖ ἡμῶν ἡ ψυχὴ τὸ σεσηπὸς σῶμα, ἀλλὰ, κἂν δέηται σώματος διὰ τὰς τοπικὰς μεταβάσεις, νοεῖ ἡ μεμελετηκυῖα τὴν „σοφίαν“ κατὰ τὸ „στόμα δικαίου μελετήσει σοφίαν“ διαφορὰν ἐπιγείου οἰκίας, ἐν ᾗ ἐστι τὸ σκῆνος, καταλυομένης καὶ σκήνους, ἐν ᾧ „οἱ ὄντες“ δίκαιοι στενάζουσι „βαρούμενοι,“ μὴ θέλοντες τὸ σκῆνος ἀπεκδύσασθαι ἀλλὰ τῷ σκήνει „ἐπενδύσασθαι,“ ἵν᾿ ἐκ τοῦ „ἐπενδύσασθαι“ „καταποθῇ τὸ θνητὸν ὑπὸ τῆς ζωῆς.“ „δεῖ γὰρ“ τῷ πᾶσαν φύσιν σώματος εἶναι φθαρτὴν „τὸ φθαρτὸν τοῦτο“ σκῆνος „ἐνδύσασθαι ἀφθαρσίαν,“ καὶ τὸ ἕτερον αὐτοῦ, τυγχάνον „θνητὸν“ καὶ δεκτικὸν τοῦ ἐπακολουθοῦντος τῷ ἁμαρτάνειν θανάτου, „ἐνδύσασθαι ἀθανασίαν“· ἵν᾿, ὅτε „τὸ φθαρτὸν“ „ἐνδύσεται τὴν ἀφθαρσίαν καὶ τὸ θνητὸν τὴν ἀθανασίαν. τότε γενήσεται“ τὸ πάλαι ὑπὸ τῶν προφητῶν προειρημένον. ἀναίρεσις τῆς νίκης τοῦ θανάτου, καθὸ νικήσας ἡμᾶς ἑαυτῷ ὑπέταξε, καὶ τοῦ ἀπ᾿ αὐτοῦ κέντρου, ᾧ κεντῶν τὴν οὐ πάντῃ πεφραγμένην ψυχὴν ἐμποιεῖ αὐτῇ τὰ ἀπὸ τῆς ἁμαρτίας τραύματα.
thought_title: Sown a natural body, raised a spiritual body
pass_a_gloss: 'God' therefore 'gives' 'to each' 'a body as he willed', as in the case of things sown, so also in the case of those as it were sown in dying (ἀποθνῄσκω) and at a fitting (ἐπιτήδειος) time (καιρός) taking up (ἀναλαμβάνω) from the things sown the 'body' put around (περιτίθημι) each according to worth (ἀξία) by God. And we hear also the word (λόγος = Scripture) teaching through more [words] the difference (διαφορά) of what is as it were sown toward what is as it were raised from it, and saying: 'It is sown in corruption (φθορά), it is raised in incorruption (ἀφθαρσία); sown in dishonour (ἀτιμία), raised in glory (δόξα); sown in weakness (ἀσθένεια), raised in power (δύναμις); sown a soul-body / natural body (σῶμα ψυχικόν), raised a spiritual body (σῶμα πνευματικόν).' Let him who is able still grasp (καταλαμβάνω) what is meant by the one saying: 'As the earthy one (χοϊκός), such also the earthy; and as the heavenly one (ἐπουράνιος), such also the heavenly. And as we bore (φορέω) the image (εἰκών) of the earthy, so let us bear (φορέσωμεν, subj.) also the image of the heavenly.' And yet, wishing to hide (κρύπτω) the secret things (ἀπόρρητα) of the passage (τόπος), not fitting (ἁρμόζω) for the simpler (ἁπλούστεροι) and the common (πάνδημος) hearing of those led to the better through believing (πιστεύω), nevertheless the apostle was compelled (ἀναγκάζω) later, so that we not mishear his words, to say after 'let us bear the image of the heavenly' the [words]: 'This I say, brothers, that flesh and blood cannot inherit (κληρονομέω) the kingdom (βασιλεία) of God, nor does corruption inherit incorruption.' Then knowing something secret and mystical (μυστικός) in the passage, as befitted (πρέπω) one leaving behind (καταλείπω) through writings (γράμματα) to those after him the things understood [as] stated, he adds and says: 'Behold, I tell you a mystery (μυστήριον)', which is customary (ἔθος) to be added to the deeper (βαθύτερα) and more mystical things, fittingly (καθηκόντως) hidden from the many (οἱ πολλοί); just as in Tobit it is written: 'A king's mystery it is good to hide', but toward the glorious (ἔνδοξος) and fitting for the many, with what is true by economy (οἰκονομικῶς ἀληθές), 'to reveal (ἀνακαλύπτω) the works of God gloriously' [is] 'good'. Not of worms (σκώληκες), then, is our hope (ἐλπίς), nor does our soul long for (ποθέω) the rotted (σήπω, pf.) body; but even if it needs (δέομαι) a body on account of movements from place to place (τοπικαὶ μεταβάσεις), the [soul] that has practised (μελετάω) 'wisdom', according to 'the mouth of a righteous man will meditate on wisdom', perceives the difference of an earthly (ἐπίγειος) house (οἰκία), in which is the tent (σκῆνος), being dissolved (καταλύω), and of the tent, in which 'those who are' righteous groan (στενάζω) 'being weighed down (βαρέω)', not wishing to strip off (ἀπεκδύομαι) the tent but to put on over (ἐπενδύομαι) the tent, so that from the 'putting on over' 'the mortal may be swallowed (καταπίνω) by life (ζωή)'. 'For it must (δεῖ)', because every nature (φύσις) of body is corruptible (φθαρτός), 'this corruptible' tent 'put on (ἐνδύω) incorruption', and the other [aspect] of it (τὸ ἕτερον αὐτοῦ), being 'mortal' (θνητός) and receptive (δεκτικός) of the death following on sinning (ἁμαρτάνω), 'put on immortality (ἀθανασία)'; so that, when 'the corruptible' 'puts on incorruption and the mortal immortality, then will come to pass' what was long ago foretold by the prophets: the taking away (ἀναίρεσις) of the victory (νίκη) of death, inasmuch as having conquered (νικάω) us it subjected (ὑποτάσσω) us to itself, and of the sting (κέντρον) from it, with which, stinging (κεντέω) the soul not wholly fenced (φράσσω), it produces in it the wounds (τραύματα) from sin (ἁμαρτία).

pass_b_english: So “God gives” “to each” “a body as he willed” (1 Corinthians 15:38): as with things that are sown, so also with those who are, as it were, sown in dying, and who at the fitting time receive from what was sown the “body” that God puts around each one according to his worth. We hear Scripture too, teaching at more length the difference between what is, so to speak, sown and what is, so to speak, raised from it, when it says: “It is sown in corruption, it is raised in incorruption; it is sown in dishonour, it is raised in glory; it is sown in weakness, it is raised in power; it is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body” (1 Corinthians 15:42–44).

Let anyone who is able go further and grasp what is meant by the one who says: “As is the one of dust, so are those who are of dust; and as is the heavenly one, so are those who are heavenly. And as we have borne the image of the one of dust, so let us also bear the image of the heavenly one” (1 Corinthians 15:48–49).

Though the apostle wished to hide the secret things of this passage, things that do not suit the simpler sort and the common hearing of those who are led to better things through believing, he was still compelled afterwards, so that we would not mishear his words, to say after “let us bear the image of the heavenly one” this: “This I say, brothers, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does corruption inherit incorruption” (1 Corinthians 15:50). Then, knowing something secret and mystical in the passage, as befitted one who was leaving his thoughts in writing for those who would come after him, he goes on to say: “Behold, I tell you a mystery” (1 Corinthians 15:51). This is the phrase usually set before things that are deeper and more mystical and are rightly hidden from the many; as it is written in Tobit: “It is good to hide a king’s mystery” (Tobit 12:7), while, with regard to what is glorious and suited to the many, together with truth given by way of accommodation, “it is good” “to reveal the works of God gloriously” (Tobit 12:7).

Our hope, then, is not the hope of worms, nor does our soul long for the body that has rotted. Even if the soul needs a body for moving from place to place, the soul that has meditated on “wisdom,” according to the words “The mouth of the righteous will meditate on wisdom” (Psalm 37:30), understands the difference between the earthly house that is being dissolved, in which the tent is, and the tent in which the righteous, “those who are” in it, groan, “being burdened,” not wishing to put off the tent but to “be clothed over” it, so that through this being “clothed over” “what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (2 Corinthians 5:1–4).

“For,” since every bodily nature is corruptible, “this corruptible” tent “must put on incorruption,” and its other aspect, which is “mortal” and liable to the death that follows on sin, must “put on immortality” (1 Corinthians 15:53); so that when “the corruptible puts on incorruption and the mortal immortality, then” there “will come to pass” (1 Corinthians 15:54) what the prophets foretold long ago: the overthrow of the victory death won when it conquered us and made us subject to itself (Isaiah 25:8), and of the sting that comes from it, with which it stings the soul that is not guarded on every side and inflicts on it the wounds that come from sin (Hosea 13:14; 1 Corinthians 15:55–56).
notes: LXX renumbering: 'The mouth of the righteous will meditate on wisdom' is LXX Psalm 36:30 = English Psalm 37:30 (LXX μελετήσει; Hebrew 'utters'); μελετάω kept as 'meditate' in both clauses to hold Origen's link. 'Not the hope of worms' and 'long for the body that has rotted' echo Celsus's words at 5.14 (σκωλήκων ἡ ἐλπίς; ποθήσειεν ἔτι σῶμα σεσηπός) but are not marked as a quotation in Origen's sentence, so they are left without quotation marks. σῶμα ψυχικόν rendered 'natural body' (literally 'soul-body', the body animated by soul); χοϊκός/ἐπουράνιος rendered 'the one of dust' / 'the heavenly one' without adding 'man'. 1 Corinthians 15:49: Origen reads the subjunctive φορέσωμεν ('let us bear'), a known variant, kept. ἀπόρρητα 'secret things'; ἁπλουστέροις rendered 'simpler believers' (the following clause names them as believers). The clause ὡς ἔπρεπε διὰ γραμμάτων καταλιπόντι τοῖς μετ᾿ αὐτὸν τὰ νενοημένα εἰρημένα is awkward in the staged text (εἰρημένα may be corrupt); rendered by sense. Tobit 12:7 (LXX; also 12:11) is quoted in two parts. οἰκονομικῶς ἀληθοῦς ('true by economy', truth adapted to the hearers' capacity in God's ordering of teaching) rendered 'truth given by way of accommodation'; doubtful nuance. 2 Corinthians 5:1–4: Origen reads ἀπεκδύσασθαι for ἐκδύσασθαι and distinguishes the 'earthly house' from the 'tent' (σκῆνος) inside it; τῷ σκήνει ἐπενδύσασθαι rendered 'be clothed over' the tent. τὸ ἕτερον αὐτοῦ ('the other [aspect] of it') rendered 'its other aspect'; Origen pairs corruptible/incorruption and mortal/immortality as two sides of the same tent. The prophecy of death's defeat is not quoted verbatim: Isaiah 25:8 (Paul's 'death is swallowed up in victory', not the LXX wording) and Hosea 13:14 ('where is your sting'), as joined in 1 Corinthians 15:54–56; cited as clear allusions. The staged text's full stop after προειρημένον stands for a colon (ἀναίρεσις is in apposition).
Open doubt (review): 5.19: εἰρημένα in ὡς ἔπρεπε ... τὰ νενοημένα εἰρημένα may be corrupt in the staged text; it is rendered by sense, as the translator noted.
Open doubt (review): 5.19: οἰκονομικῶς ἀληθοῦς is rendered 'truth given by way of accommodation'; the exact shade is open to interpretation, though the reading is defensible.
